after: ## Drawing ray diagrams that earn the marks
alt: Left: a ray reflects from a mirror with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection, both measured from the dashed normal. Right: a ray passing from air into glass slows and bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence.
caption: Measure all angles from the normal; light entering glass bends towards it.

after: ## The refraction practical with three block shapes (3.17)
alt: Rectangular block: the ray bends towards the normal entering and away leaving, so it emerges parallel to the incident ray but shifted. Semi-circular block: the ray enters the curved side along a radius without bending and refracts only at the flat face. Triangular prism: the ray is deviated towards the base and white light spreads into colours.
caption: Each block shape shows something different: a parallel shift, one clean refraction, or dispersion.

after: ## Measuring the refractive index of glass (3.18, 3.19)
alt: A graph of sin i against sin r with five plotted points and a straight line of best fit through the origin. Using the points (0.225, 0.342) and (0.574, 0.866), the gradient is 0.524 ÷ 0.349 = 1.50, the refractive index.
caption: Plot sin i against sin r: the gradient is the refractive index, n = 1.50.

after: ## Total internal reflection and the critical angle (3.20 to 3.22)
alt: Acrylic with refractive index 1.49 has a critical angle of 42.2°. A ray inside a semicircular acrylic block meeting the flat surface at 40° refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal; a ray at 50° is totally internally reflected.
caption: Below the critical angle light escapes; above it, all of it reflects.

after: ## Total internal reflection and the critical angle (3.20 to 3.22)
alt: A ray zig-zags along a glass fibre, meeting the side wall each time at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again and stays inside.
caption: Every bounce is total internal reflection, so the light follows the fibre.

alt: Echo method: a person 80 m from a wall claps in time with the echoes; 20 intervals take 9.6 s, so one interval is 0.48 s, the sound travels 160 m and the speed is 330 m/s. Second method: two microphones a measured distance apart record the time delay.
caption: The echo travels to the wall and back: speed = 2 × 80 ÷ 0.48 = 330 m/s.

alt: An oscilloscope screen of 10 divisions showing a trace in which one complete wave spans 5.0 divisions. With a timebase of 0.20 ms per division the period is 1.0 ms, so the frequency is 1 ÷ 0.0010 = 1000 Hz.
caption: Divisions per wave × timebase = period; frequency = 1 ÷ period.
